meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RAs were compared against first-line mild diabetes therapy (metformin monotherapy) and end-stage therapy (insulin monotherapy) without adequate control for diabetes duration, baseline glycemic severity (HbA1c was missing in 91.27% of participants), or renal baseline parameters, producing extreme hazard ratios for unrelated outcomes (such as leukemia sHR 15.09, 95% CI: 4.65–48.98 and acute nephritis sHR 4.11, 95% CI: 2.21–7.64) that reflect severe residual confounding by indication and surveillance.

findings.title: Severe unmeasured confounding and missing key clinical covariates
findings.mechanism: Matching included missing values as explicit dummy categories (e.g., BMI missing in 32.49% to 36.08%, age missing in ~20%, education missing in ~33%), while key clinical determinants such as HbA1c (missing >90%) and disease duration were not properly adjusted, leaving substantial imbalance between treatment arms.

overall.summary: This retrospective observational cohort study exhibits a very high overall risk of bias across multiple ROBINS-E domains. Critical clinical confounders—notably baseline HbA1c (missing in >91% of participants), disease duration, and baseline organ function—were either missing or adjusted by matching on an 'unspecified' category. Furthermore, the cohort definition relied on maintaining monotherapy throughout follow-up, and outcome ascertainment via EHR text/ICD-10 searches was highly vulnerable to surveillance and detection bias for conditions with existing drug safety alerts (pancreatitis, thyroid disorders, acute kidney injury). These methodological flaws strongly threaten the validity of the reported causal conclusions.

baseline_comparability.summary: Baseline demographic comparisons show that GLP-1 RA users were significantly younger and had higher rates of obesity, higher education, and citizen health insurance compared to metformin and insulin users. The observation of higher rates of kidney failure, cancer, and nephritis in a notably younger cohort suggests substantial confounding by indication, unmeasured diabetes duration, and surveillance/detection bias.
